```{r setup, include = FALSE}
has_data <- requireNamespace("StMoMo", quietly = TRUE)
has_gg <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE) && has_data
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, eval = has_data, message = FALSE)
```

Official tables often give deaths in 5-year age groups and populations by
single year of age. Many models are easiest to use on single years. There
are two ways to bring the two together:

* **regroup** everything to the age groups of the deaths
  (`mt_regroup(x, age = "deaths")`) and model the groups; nothing is
  estimated, but the age detail is lost;
* **ungroup** the deaths: estimate single-year deaths from the observed
  groups (`mt_ungroup()`).

This vignette compares the ungrouping methods, shows the diagnostics that
check a result, and the consequence for a forecast. The test case is data
whose single years are known: England & Wales men, 1980-2011, ages 30-99
(Human Mortality Database, via the StMoMo package). Their deaths are grouped
as an official table would group them, ungrouped again, and compared with
what was observed.

```{r}
library(mortensor)
ew <- as_mt_data(StMoMo::EWMaleData)
ew <- mt_subset(ew, ages = c(30, 100), periods = c(1980, 2011))
x <- mt_regroup(ew, age = c(seq(30, 85, 5), 90), measures = "deaths")
x
```

The deaths are now in the groups 30-34, ..., 85-89 and 90-99; the
exposures keep their single years (`measures = "deaths"` regroups only the
deaths). HMD data downloaded directly are read with `mt_read_hmd()`.

## The methods

| `method` | Idea | Needs exposures |
|---|---|---|
| `"pclm"` (default) | penalized composite link model (Eilers 2007; Rizzi et al. 2015): a smooth rate schedule whose expected deaths, summed over each group, are fitted to the group totals; the exposures enter as offset | yes (or ungroups counts) |
| `"monotone"` | monotone cubic interpolation of the cumulative deaths (Hyman 1983), counts only | no |

With `dims = 2`, the PCLM estimates a smooth surface over age and year
instead of each year separately. The PCLM estimates rates, so the
irregular sizes of birth cohorts stay in the exposures; the monotone
spline splits the counts and does not use the exposures. The methods
`"hyman_kannisto"`, `"natural_gompertz"` and `"gam"` are deprecated: they
are heuristics of this package without a published source, and they still
work with a warning.

```{r}
u <- list("PCLM" = mt_ungroup(x), "monotone" = mt_ungroup(x, method = "monotone"))
```

## Diagnostic 1: do the estimates pass through the groups?

The observed rates of the age groups (grey steps) and the ungrouped
single-year rates in 2011:

```{r, eval = has_gg}
mt_plot_ungroup(x, u, period = 2011)
```

Both pass through the steps and agree up to age 90. In the last group
nothing in the data says how the rates rise between ages 90 and 99: the
PCLM continues the rise of the rates below 90, while the monotone spline of
the cumulative deaths lets the rates rise and then fall towards 99.

## Diagnostic 2: errors against the known single years

`mt_ungroup_check()` compares the estimates with the known rates by age
band. `mae_log` is the median absolute log error (close to the relative
error for small values). The known rates contain Poisson noise, so even
perfect estimates would not reach zero: `noise_log` is the error that
perfect estimates would have. `bias_log` is the median signed error, and
`max_rel_gap` the largest relative difference between the estimated and
the observed group totals.

```{r}
mt_ungroup_check(u, reference = ew)
```

In every age band the errors of the PCLM exceed the noise floor by at
most 0.3 percentage points: its rates are almost as close to the observed
single years as the true rates would be. The PCLM does not reproduce each
group total exactly; here it misses them by up to 2.6%. The monotone
spline reproduces the totals exactly, but its errors exceed the noise floor
by 1.1 and 1.4 percentage points at ages 45-64 and 65-84 and by 5.3 points
at 85 and over: it splits the deaths without the exposures, so the
irregular sizes of birth cohorts within a group end up in the rates. Where
the methods differ shows in the log ratio of the estimated to the known
rates by age, with its range over the years (coloured) and the range of
the Poisson noise (grey):

```{r, eval = has_gg}
mt_plot_ungroup(x, u, type = "error", reference = ew)
```

Up to age 95 the PCLM estimates scatter within the noise band; at the top
of the last group they overestimate the rates at 99 by about 7%. The
monotone spline falls far below the known rates above age 95. An open or
wide last group is where ungrouping is least reliable, and where methods
should be compared.

## Diagnostic 3: stability over time

Ungrouping each year separately (`dims = 1`) can let single ages jump from
year to year. The two-dimensional PCLM (`dims = 2`) smooths over the years
as well. It is slower, so the comparison uses 2000-2011:

```{r}
xr <- mt_subset(x, periods = c(2000, 2011))
u_time <- list("PCLM 1D" = mt_ungroup(xr), "PCLM 2D" = mt_ungroup(xr, dims = 2))
mt_ungroup_check(u_time, reference = ew)
```

```{r, eval = has_gg, fig.height = 3.5}
mt_plot_ungroup(xr, u_time, type = "time", reference = ew)
```

The lines are the ungrouped rates at four ages, the points the known rates.
Both versions follow the trend of the known rates. For these large counts
the difference between 1D and 2D is small; it matters more for small
populations, where the 2D surface borrows strength from neighbouring
years. The 2D surface misses the group totals by more (up to 7.0%,
against 1.8% in 1D), because it also smooths over the years.

The estimates are the fitted values of the PCLM, as published. With
`preserve_totals = TRUE`, `mt_ungroup()` rescales the estimates within
each group to the observed total after the fit. This rescaling is
specific to this package (reference unknown): it creates steps at the group
boundaries, and in 2D it puts the year-to-year noise of every group back
onto the smooth surface. Inside backtests, ungrouping in 2D must see only
the training years: use `step_ungroup(dims = 2)` in the preprocessing.

## Grouped exposures

When the populations are grouped as well, they are ungrouped first, as
counts (`exposure_method = "pclm"`) or by a monotone spline of the
cumulative counts (`"monotone"`, which reproduces the group totals
exactly). Here the exposures are grouped and the deaths kept by single
year, so the errors of the rates come from the exposures alone:

```{r}
xe <- mt_regroup(ew, age = c(seq(30, 85, 5), 90), measures = "exposure")
mt_ungroup_check(list("PCLM" = mt_ungroup(xe), "monotone" = mt_ungroup(xe, exposure_method = "monotone")),
                 reference = ew)
```

Below age 85 both methods err by 1-2%, which at ages 65-84 is more than
the noise of the deaths. At ages 85 and over, where the population falls
steeply with age, the PCLM errs by about 6% and the monotone spline by
about 16%. Splitting an **open** interval of
populations (for example 85+ into single years up to 100+) from its total
alone is not reliable at all: use population data with a higher open age,
which many statistical offices publish, or keep the open interval.

## The consequence for a forecast

Lee-Carter fitted to the age groups, to the PCLM estimates and to the known
single years, forecast to 2031. Life expectancy at 30 sums over all ages,
so it is the quantity least affected by the details within a group:

```{r}
fc <- list("age groups" = mt_forecast(mt_fit(lee_carter(), mt_regroup(x, age = "deaths")), h = 20, n_draws = 500,
                                      seed = 1),
           "PCLM single years" = mt_forecast(mt_fit(lee_carter(), u$PCLM), h = 20, n_draws = 500, seed = 1),
           "known single years" = mt_forecast(mt_fit(lee_carter(), ew), h = 20, n_draws = 500, seed = 1))
mt_compare_forecasts(fc, periods = c(2021, 2031), digits = 2)
```

```{r, eval = has_gg, fig.height = 4}
mt_plot_compare(fc, quantity = "rate", ages = c("92", "95"), periods = 2001:2031)
```

Forecasts from the PCLM estimates and from the known single years give
life expectancies at 30 within 0.01 years of each other. The forecast from
the age groups is 0.4 years higher: its life table assumes that the deaths
of each group fall in the middle of the group, which overstates survival
where mortality rises steeply within a group, above all in the 10-year
group 90-99. The single-year rates at 92 and 95 forecast from the PCLM
estimates follow those from the known rates closely; a model of the groups
has no rates for single ages at all (the figure shows only the two
single-year forecasts). Ungrouping is worth its assumptions where single
ages are needed: for life tables of wide groups, for cohort models, or for
results at exact ages.

## Summary

* Ungroup deaths as rates, with the exposures on the target grid as offset
  (`mt_ungroup()`, PCLM by default). The estimates are the fitted values
  of the PCLM; `preserve_totals = TRUE` rescales them to the group totals
  (a step of this package).
* Check every result: `mt_plot_ungroup()` (profile, errors, stability over
  time) and `mt_ungroup_check()` (fit diagnostics, and errors where single
  years are known).
* The last, wide or open age group is where methods differ; compare them
  there.
* Inside forecasting pipelines, ungrouping is a preprocessing step
  (`step_ungroup()`), refitted on each training window.

## References

Eilers PHC (2007). Ill-posed problems with counts, the composite link model
and penalized likelihood. *Statistical Modelling* 7(3): 239-254.

Hyman JM (1983). Accurate monotonicity preserving cubic interpolation.
*SIAM Journal on Scientific and Statistical Computing* 4(4): 645-654.

Rizzi S, Gampe J, Eilers PHC (2015). Efficient estimation of smooth
distributions from coarsely grouped data. *American Journal of
Epidemiology* 182(2): 138-147.
